PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THE ICH E9(R1) ADDENDUM (SECTION A.1) Randomised controlled trials are generally considered to be the optimal experimental design to minimise the biases when estimating treatment effects to investigate the effects of medical interventions.1and2 They are typically conducted to compare the effect of two or more assigned treatment options, one (or more) under investigation and the other one(s) as standard of care or placebo. The current ICH E92 guideline describing statistical principles for clinical trials presents us with two main analysis sets that define which patients should be included in the analysis. Similar assumptions are made with multiple imputation methods, with the additional complication that the details of such procedures are nearly always under‐reported.3 It is often believed that analyses conducted in line with the ITT principle estimate the effect of treatment assignment in practical clinical scenarios.4 However, in the case where patients are discontinuing treatment for adverse events (AE) without having their follow‐up data collected, the effect that is actually estimated should be interpreted as “the effect of treatment assignment until having to stop randomised treatment due to AE” or “the effect of treatment assignment assuming that patients retain the benefits from treatment after having to stop for AE”. 2. Title: An adaptive imputation method of missing data for sparsely retrieved dropouts in treatment policy strategy - ScienceDirect
# An adaptive imputation method of missing data for sparsely retrieved dropouts in treatment policy strategy. After discontinuing treatment, participants who remain in the trial to complete the assessment of the primary endpoints are referred to as retrieved dropouts, while early withdrawal by participants results in missing data. To mitigate the effects of missing data, strategies like mixed model for repeated measures or the retrieved dropout multiple imputation method are used. This article introduces an innovative adaptive model that refines the On/Off Intercepts with Common Slopes using Residuals (RD\_OICSR) model, which is a model within the retrieved dropout methods, and evaluates it using simulated data from a depression trial. Therefore, strategies for handling intercurrent events, along with appropriate methods for addressing missing data, should be predefined in accordance with the trial's objectives. The strategy for handling intercurrent events defines which observed data should be included in the analysis and which should be considered missing, making it crucial for this approach to align with the trial's objectives [3,4]. When applied to the treatment policy, this method uses all available data, regardless of whether participants experience an intercurrent event, under the assumption that the missing data mechanism is Missing at Random (MAR). Additionally, missing data can be modeled and imputed by either using only the data from participants who experienced intercurrent events, or by marking the data of these participants as treatment-compliant and including all their data in the analysis. Once the missing data has been imputed, analysis is performed on the complete dataset using ANCOVA or other methods, and Rubin's rules are applied to summarize results and estimate treatment efficacy. The treatment policy estimand, a specific form of de facto estimand, incorporates data from all participants experiencing intercurrent events, whether they continue or discontinue treatment, without treating post-event data as missing. In treatment policy strategies, when the missing data mechanisms after intercurrent events are MCAR or MAR, RDs-based methods for handling missing data are highly accurate. ### Estimating and reporting treatment effects in clinical trials for weight management: using estimands to interpret effects of intercurrent events and missing data. Complete case analysis (CCA) is the most common method used to handle missing outcome data in trials but may often lead to biased estimates.

results.title: Estimating and reporting treatment effects in clinical trials for weight management: using estimands to interpret effects of intercurrent events and missing data - PMC
results.content: # Estimating and reporting treatment effects in clinical trials for weight management: using estimands to interpret effects of intercurrent events and missing data. Usually, as with other drug evaluations, the placebo-adjusted treatment effect (i.e., the difference between weight losses with pharmacotherapy and placebo, when given as an adjunct to lifestyle intervention) is provided from data in randomized clinical trials (RCTs). This article reviews how intercurrent events during weight management trials can influence placebo-adjusted treatment effects, depending on how they are accounted for and how missing data are handled. Similarly, clinical trial programs for weight management drugs in development, such as the semaglutide 2.4 mg once-weekly STEP (Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with obesity) trial program [9–16] are planned to report results utilizing estimands. In this review, we discuss how intercurrent events can affect the estimation and interpretation/quantification of a treatment effect in weight management trials; how approaches for handling missing data have evolved over the last decade; and implications for interpreting clinical data from weight management RCTs. We examine these issues using the SCALE phase 3a clinical trial program as an example and address how the use of estimands may help provide greater transparency in clinical trial reporting. With the increasing computational awareness and capacity to develop statistical methods that provide more useful interpretations of the treatment effect, MI methods have become dominant for the reporting of recent weight management clinical trials (e.g., semaglutide obesity phase 2 trial [34] and the SCALE phase 3b trials [7, 8]). Regardless of the assumption used to impute missing values, the MI approach is considered valid to evaluate a placebo-adjusted weight loss for a *treatment policy estimate* because all available data are used irrespective of what happens to the participants in the trial (i.e., ignoring intercurrent events). In the phase 3a SCALE trials, participants’ body weight loss with liraglutide 3.0 mg treatment was 6.0–8.0% reported using a LOCF-based analysis method [26, 27, 32] and 4.9–7.4% using MI [37]. To provide different perspectives on the estimated treatment effect in weight management RCTs, we recommend that future publications investigating new or already-approved weight-loss medications report the *treatment policy estimand* and the *trial product estimand*.

results.title: Applying the Estimand Framework to Non‐Inferiority Trials - Lynggaard - 2024 - Pharmaceutical Statistics - Wiley Online Library
results.content: The International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use notes in their addendum on estimands and sensitivity analysis in clinical trials that there may be special considerations to the implementation of estimands in clinical trials with a non-inferiority objective yet provides little guidance. The ICH E9(R1) addendum [1] does not specify which estimands are appropriate in a non-inferiority setting but notes ‘Estimands that are constructed with one or more intercurrent events accounted for using the treatment policy strategy present similar issues for non-inferiority and equivalence trials as those related to analysis of the FAS under the ITT principle. There is also a note of warning when determining the non-inferiority margin from estimated effect sizes from completed trials, since consistent definitions of estimands, particularly the handling of intercurrent events, will need consideration. For example, in a non-inferiority trial where the interest is in the population of patients who would have the intercurrent events neither under the test treatment nor the reference treatment, for the non-inferiority margin to be appropriate, it would need to be determined based on the effect of the reference treatment versus placebo in the population of interest defined by the principal stratum for which generally no studies are available. In clinical trials with both non-inferiority and superiority objectives, a key aspect is whether the non-inferiority and superiority claims are to be made for the same estimand, that is for the same treatment condition(s), the same population, the same variable and population-level summary as well as the same intercurrent events handling strategies. The EMA Guideline on clinical investigation of medicinal products in the treatment or prevention of diabetes mellitus [16] states that the same attributes may be used: ‘For active controlled trials with a non-inferiority (NI) hypothesis, the same primary estimand strategy as outlined above might be justified […] Furthermore, it is likely necessary that a supplemental estimand is specified to address the impact of important intercurrent events like protocol violations and deviations’. R. Carpenter, “Handling Intercurrent Events and Missing Data in Non-Inferiority Trials Using the Estimand Framework: A Tuberculosis Case Study,” *Clinical Trials* 20, no.
